displayQuote: Neither a borrower nor a lender be

meta.title: Who really said "Neither a borrower nor a lender be"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Scripture. Polonius says it in Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 3 — and the 1604 Second Quarto reads "a lender, boy" and "love oft loses."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Neither a borrower nor a lender be'?
meta.ogDescription: There is no such Bible verse. The line is Polonius's in Shakespeare's Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 3, and the early printed texts do not agree on its wording.

answer.label: Not the Bible — William Shakespeare
answer.sourceLine: The line is spoken by Polonius in Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3, as he sends his son Laertes off to France — not by any biblical writer. It is absent from the 1603 First Quarto, appears in the 1604 Second Quarto as “Neither a borrower nor a lender, boy,” and reaches its familiar form in the 1623 First Folio.

source.heading: The passage

docMeta.dd: Second Quarto, 1604 (absent from the 1603 First Quarto)

source.excerpt: Neither a borrower nor a lender be: / For loan oft loses both itself and friend; / And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry. / This above all: to thine own self be true; / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man.
trail: The 1603 First Quarto ↗ gives the farewell precepts to Corambis, and they contain no borrower-and-lender couplet — the speech runs from “Be thou familiar, but by no meanes vulgare” to “This aboue all, to thy owne selfe be true.”

The couplet appears in the 1604 Second Quarto ↗, but in a different form: “Neither a borrower nor a lender, boy, / For love oft loses both itself and friend, / And borrowing dulleth edge of husbandry.”
The wording that became proverbial is the 1623 First Folio’s ↗: “Neither a borrower, nor a lender be; / For lone oft loses both it selfe and friend.”
Wikiquote’s sourced Hamlet page ↗ cites the line at Act I, scene iii, lines 75–76, spoken by Polonius.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text. The 1623 First Folio prints it as “Neither a borrower, nor a lender be; / For lone oft loses both it selfe and friend: / And borrowing duls the edge of Husbandry.”

source.rightsNote: Hamlet was printed in 1603, 1604 and 1623, all centuries before the 1931 US copyright threshold, and Shakespeare died in 1616. The play’s text is firmly in the public domain worldwide; note that individual modern editions — their notes, glosses and editorial emendations — can carry their own copyright, even though the dialogue itself does not.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: William Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around the turn of the seventeenth century; it survives in three early printings that do not agree with one another — the short First Quarto of 1603, the fuller Second Quarto of 1604, and the First Folio of 1623. The borrower-and-lender couplet belongs to Polonius, the king’s elderly counsellor, and is part of a string of copybook maxims he unloads on his departing son. Shakespeare gives the speech to a character the play repeatedly shows to be a meddler and a windbag, which is why editors have argued for centuries about how straight the advice is meant to be taken.

misattribution.heading: What the record actually shows
misattribution.intro: The couplet is quoted as though it were proverbial Scripture. It is a line of dramatic dialogue, and even its wording is not quite what most people repeat.

items.why: Scripture contains no verse of this wording or this sense. The Bible warns about the position of the debtor — Proverbs 22:7 ↗, “the borrower is servant to the lender” — but it never counsels against lending. Deuteronomy 15:8 ↗ commands the reverse: “thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need.”

The words are Polonius’s, delivered as parting advice to Laertes in Act 1, Scene 3 — a character the play presents, in one commentator’s phrase, as a pompous buffoon with little self-awareness ↗. Shakespeare wrote the line; he did not necessarily endorse it.

The version everyone quotes is the First Folio’s. The 1604 Second Quarto ↗ instead reads “Neither a borrower nor a lender, boy, / For love oft loses both itself and friend, / And borrowing dulleth edge of husbandry.”

The couplet is missing from the earliest printed Hamlet altogether: in the 1603 First Quarto ↗ the precepts are given by Corambis to Leartes and run from “Be thou familiar, but by no meanes vulgare” straight through to “This aboue all, to thy owne selfe be true” with no borrower-and-lender lines.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote it, Polonius says it, and it is in Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 3 ↗ — not in the Bible.

context.heading: Why the mix-up is so durable
lead: The couplet does everything a proverb is supposed to do: it scans, it balances, and it sounds like received wisdom rather than one man’s opinion. Filed alongside “to thine own self be true” — which comes four lines later in the same speech — it acquires the tone of Scripture without any of the substance, and gets quoted in sermons, financial-advice columns and greetings cards as though it had chapter and verse behind it.

It does not. The Bible is wary of debt — Proverbs 22:7 observes that “the borrower is servant to the lender” — but it never tells anyone to stop lending. Deuteronomy 15:8 commands the opposite: “thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need.” Polonius’s advice and Scripture’s point in different directions.
detailsBody: Shakespeare puts the maxim in the mouth of a character the play treats with steady irony. Polonius spies on his own children, hides behind a curtain to eavesdrop, and is stabbed through it. Reading his precepts as the author’s own settled philosophy is a choice, not a given — and it is a choice the couplet’s afterlife as free-floating “wisdom” quietly makes for the reader.
context.pull: Polonius is not a prophet. He is a courtier giving his son a lecture at the door.

sourcesVerified.claim: Polonius's speech in Hamlet Act 1, Scene 3 contains "Neither a borrower nor a lender be: For loan oft loses both itself and friend; And borrowing dulls the edge of husbandry," followed by "This above all: to thine own self be true."
Project Gutenberg's Hamlet (eBook #1524) carries the same passage verbatim through "Thou canst not then be false to any man."

The 1623 First Folio text prints "Neither a borrower, nor a lender be; / For lone oft loses both it selfe and friend: / And borrowing duls the edge of Husbandry. / This aboue all; to thine owne selfe be true."

The 1604 Second Quarto reads "Neither a borrower nor a lender, boy, / For love oft loses both itself and friend, / And borrowing dulleth edge of husbandry" — i.e. "boy" for "be" and "love" for "loan."

The 1603 First Quarto gives the precepts speech to Corambis addressing Leartes and contains no line resembling "Neither a borrower nor a lender be," while still ending "This aboue all, to thy owne selfe be true."
Wikiquote's sourced Hamlet page cites the line at Act I, scene iii, lines 75–76, spoken by Polonius.
Proverbs 22:7 (KJV) reads "The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender."
Deuteronomy 15:8 (KJV) reads "But thou shalt open thine hand wide unto him, and shalt surely lend him sufficient for his need, in that which he wanteth."
The phrase originates in Shakespeare's Hamlet and is spoken by Lord Polonius.
Polonius utters the line in Act 1 Scene 3 while bidding farewell to Laertes, and the play presents him as "a pompous buffoon with little self-awareness."
The line comes from Shakespeare's Hamlet rather than Scripture, though the Bible warns about debt (Proverbs 22:7, Deuteronomy 28:44, Psalm 37:21).
